aircraft.name: Aero 5 Inch
aircraft.blurb: Your 5-inch speed design: 263 mm carbon X-frame inside an aero shell, 400 mm body, launched off its tail. 1.1 kg, 6.6:1, and it runs out of pack before it runs out of speed.
aircraft.author: RealPapaNerf

aircraft.name: Blown-wing VTOL
aircraft.blurb: Twin-motor flying wing that stands on its tail. The two props blow over the elevons, which is the only thing holding its attitude at zero airspeed — then it tips over and flies away as a wing at 97 km/h.
aircraft.author: Flightline

aircraft.name: 2 m camera platform
aircraft.blurb: Two-metre pod-and-boom camera plane, 3 kg, flaps over most of the span and retracts. Slow, steady and happy to be left alone — the Ranger 1980 / Skywalker 1900 idea.
aircraft.author: Flightline

aircraft.name: 7" lifting body
aircraft.blurb: 7-inch long-range quad with a 345 mm wing across the frame, rigged 32° up from the props. 1.2 kg on 6S2P Li-ion: the wing carries about a quarter of the weight at cruise and the range goes up by a quarter with it.
aircraft.author: Flightline

aircraft.name: Nano Goblin · ArduPilot
aircraft.blurb: The 580 mm plank with an ArduPilot stack, GPS mast and a downward lidar: 300 g instead of 250, so it stalls a little faster and climbs a little worse. Turn the lidar on under Link & sensors.
aircraft.author: RealPapaNerf

aircraft.name: 10" GEPRC Mark4
aircraft.blurb: 10-inch Mark4 LR on a 6S2P 18650 pack, 1.55 kg, about 5:1. Long range, tilting camera mount, and enough prop to carry something.
aircraft.author: RealPapaNerf

aircraft.name: 13" recovery quad
aircraft.blurb: 13-inch lifter on 12S2P 21700 Li-ion with landing gear and the three-camera pod. 3.7 kg, about 4.6:1. Long legs, slow props and a lot of momentum.
aircraft.author: RealPapaNerf

aircraft.name: 7" quad · ArduPilot
aircraft.blurb: 7-inch long-range quad with an ArduPilot stack on a 6S2P 18650 pack. 1.15 kg, about 6:1 on the motor rating — but the pack cannot feed a full punch, so watch what the voltage does when you pull hard.
aircraft.author: RealPapaNerf

aircraft.name: Speed tail-sitter
aircraft.blurb: Four motors along the nose, a body that flies like a wing, and nothing else. Stands on its tail, pitches over, and runs.
aircraft.author: Flightline

aircraft.name: Tip-prop heli
aircraft.blurb: 2.6 kg camera helicopter with a 1.5 m rotor driven by two 5-inch props out at the blades — no tail rotor, because tip drive reacts on the air and not on the airframe. The pedal is a motor on the mast, so it steers on the rotor’s inertia and spends headspeed doing it. A derotated camera rides the hub.
aircraft.author: Flightline

aircraft.name: Autogyro
aircraft.blurb: 3.2 kg autogyro: a 1.7 m rotor nobody drives, a pusher prop, and a mast raked 9° back so the air keeps the head turning. Prerotate on the ground, roll, fly. Every landing is an autorotation, which is why gyro pilots are good at them.
aircraft.author: Flightline

aircraft.name: Gyrodyne
aircraft.blurb: 4.5 kg helicopter–autogyro hybrid: a 1.7 m shaft-driven rotor, no tail rotor, and two reversing-pitch tractor props on stub wings countering the torque between them. Throttle hold tilts the head back and it becomes an autogyro; let it off and it is a helicopter again.
aircraft.author: Flightline

aircraft.name: Prandtl-D
aircraft.blurb: 3.75 m bell-spanload flying wing with no fin at all. The washout is derived, not guessed: the outer 30% of the span flies in upwash and makes induced thrust, so it yaws into its own roll instead of away from it. Turn on Sim rules → Accurate aerodynamics or none of that is there.
aircraft.author: Flightline

aircraft.name: Heli 600 DD
aircraft.blurb: 600-size electric helicopter, direct drive: a huge slow outrunner bolted straight to the head, no gearbox anywhere. Built part-by-part in Whirligig and exported; about 4 kg.
aircraft.author: Whirligig

aircraft.name: Tipjet
aircraft.blurb: Tip-drive helicopter from Whirligig: the shaft is free — no motor on it anywhere — and the head is driven entirely by two small props out at 92% radius, so there is no torque to counter and no tail rotor.
aircraft.author: Whirligig

aircraft.name: Tri-blade
aircraft.blurb: The Nick Rehm machine from Whirligig: three wings that are also rotor blades, each carrying its own motor and prop mid-span, exported as a tip-drive heli.
aircraft.author: Whirligig

aircraft.name: Stop-rotor
aircraft.blurb: The helicopter half of Whirligig's stop-rotor machine: a tip-prop head and a pusher. The stop-the-rotor-and-fly-on-the-blades trick does not project onto Flightline, so here it stays a tip-drive heli.
aircraft.author: Whirligig

aircraft.name: Whirligig autogyro
aircraft.blurb: Whirligig's 2 kg autogyro — smaller and lighter than Flightline's own: free teetering head on a 9° raked mast, pusher prop, electric pre-rotator that drops out before the roll.
aircraft.author: Whirligig

aircraft.name: Whirligig gyrodyne
aircraft.blurb: Whirligig's gyrodyne capstone: driven rotor in heli mode, free in autogyro mode, tip props on stub wings holding the torque. Its mode crossfade is mapped onto Flightline's own heli→autogyro transition.
aircraft.author: Whirligig

aircraft.name: Quad 7in
aircraft.blurb: Whirligig's 725 g 7-inch baseline on 4S Li-ion, thrust estimated by momentum theory — worth flying against the native 7-inch quads to see how the two models compare.
aircraft.author: Whirligig

aircraft.name: Tiltrotor
aircraft.blurb: Whirligig's tandem-wing quad tiltrotor, exported as a plain quad in hover trim — tilt servos do not translate, so the forward-flight half of its life stays in Whirligig.
aircraft.author: Whirligig
